name: The mind's mechanisms
draftedBy: Claude, 15 Nov 2026, from Bryan's words the same day: "sunk cost fallacies cognitive dissonance et cetera ... people don't know how these affect things. These mechanisms are so vital for so much." The draft list is docs/MIND-MECHANISMS-draft.md. Every line here waits for Bryan to keep, change or strike.
why: Your mind runs on shortcuts. Most of the time they help. Some of them cost you money, time and years, and the people selling to you know them better than you do.
outcomes: Spot the sunk cost trap, and choose by what is ahead instead of what is already spent.
Notice when you are changing the story to stop a clash, instead of changing what you do.
Feel the pull of "only today" and "everyone is going", and still take the time to choose.

Ask whether you would choose what you have if you were choosing today.

units.title: Sunk cost
units.outcome: Spot the sunk cost trap, and choose by what is ahead instead of what is already spent.
units.why: Money, time and effort you already spent are gone whichever way you choose. Letting them pick for you means paying again for something already lost.
units.reachesYou: The car you keep fixing, the job you stay in because of the years you put in, the course you finish though it stopped helping, the plate you clean though you are full.
units.do: Pick one thing you keep doing mostly because of what you already put in. Ask: if I were starting fresh today, with nothing spent, would I choose this? Write the answer down.

scene.analogy: Staying through a bad movie because you paid
map: paying again for what is gone

actors.label: "I paid for it, so I'll stay."

beats.say: Thirty minutes in, it is bad.
The only real choice: what comes next.

film.label: The bad deal
film.sub: the job, the car, the plan

beats.say: Spent is spent. Choose what's ahead.

units.title: Cognitive dissonance
units.outcome: Notice when you are changing the story to stop a clash, instead of changing what you do.
units.why: When two of your thoughts clash, like "I chose well" and "this is not working", it feels bad. The fastest way to stop the feeling is to change the story. The fact stays where it was.
units.reachesYou: Defending a car, a candidate, a partner or a plan long after it stopped working, because admitting it would mean you chose wrong.
units.do: Find one thing you defend a little too hard. Say out loud: "I chose that, and it is not working." Notice the sting, and notice that nothing bad happened.

scene.analogy: New shoes that pinch, called comfy
map: the fact that it is not working
the story that stops the clash

beats.say: So you change the story, not the shoes.

shoe.label: Your choice
shoe.sub: a plan, a vote, a buy

beats.say: Fix the shoe, not the story.

units.title: Fear of missing out
units.outcome: Feel the pull of "only today" and "everyone is going", and still take the time to choose.
units.why: A closing door makes anything look more valuable. Sellers and apps close doors on purpose, so you decide before you think.
units.reachesYou: "Sale ends tonight", "only 2 left", countdown timers, the group chat everyone is in, scrolling at 2 AM so you don't miss a post.
units.do: Next time something says "only today", wait one day. Write down whether you still want it, and whether the deal really ended.

map: buying what you did not need
the deal that always comes back

beats.say: The elevator doors start to close.
Sales and feeds work the same way.

units.title: Confirmation bias
units.outcome: Look for what would prove you wrong, not only for what agrees with you.
units.why: Once you believe something, you look where it will be confirmed and skip where it might not. Each look feels like proof. It is the same room, searched again.
units.reachesYou: The feed that only shows what you already like, the friend you ask because you know their answer, the reviews you read only after you bought it.
units.do: Pick one thing you are sure of. Find the best case against it, written by someone who knows the subject. Read it to the end before you answer it.

scene.analogy: Searching for your keys only where you hope they are

beats.say: You search it. Again. And again.
They were in your coat all along.
Look where you hope it isn't.

units.title: Anchoring
units.outcome: Notice when the first number you heard is setting the price, and set your own first.
units.why: The first number you hear becomes the ruler you measure everything after it with, even when that number was made up. Sellers say theirs first for a reason.
units.reachesYou: Car stickers, "was $90", the first offer in a raise talk, a hospital bill you negotiate down, a home's asking price.
units.do: Before your next big purchase or pay talk, write down what you think it is worth, from your own research, before you hear their number.

scene.analogy: Haggling down from the sticker on a car

beats.say: The first number pulls every number after it.

units.title: Loss aversion
units.outcome: Weigh a possible loss and an equal gain on the same scale.
units.why: Losing something hurts about twice as much as gaining the same thing feels good. So people pass up good chances to avoid small risks, and hold on to bad ones to avoid admitting a loss.
units.reachesYou: Staying in a job you have outgrown, keeping a stock that keeps falling, buying the extended warranty, "free trial" offers that count on you hating to lose what you already have.
units.do: Think of one change you keep putting off. Write the best thing that could come of it and the worst. Read them as the same size. Which is bigger now?

map: how much more a loss weighs

beats.say: Same money. The loss hurts about twice as much.
So you dodge risks you should take.
Jobs, moves, money: the same scale.

units.title: Availability
units.outcome: Tell how often something happens from how easy it is to picture.
units.why: Your mind judges how likely something is by how fast an example comes to mind. Loud, rare, scary things come to mind fast. Quiet, common dangers do not.
units.reachesYou: Fearing planes but not cars, buying lottery tickets after a winner is on the news, worrying about strangers while the real risks sit at home: the stairs, the pool, the car.
units.do: Pick one thing you worry about. Look up how many people it actually hurts in a year, then look up one ordinary thing you do daily. Compare the two numbers.

scene.analogy: Afraid of sharks, not the drive to the beach
map: the danger that is easy to picture

beats.say: A shark attack is on the news. All week.
You drive there without a thought.
The drive is the real danger.
Check the numbers, not the noise.

units.title: Bandwagon
units.outcome: Tell "many people chose it" apart from "it is good".
units.why: A crowd is a quick signal, and sometimes a good one. But a line can form just because there was already a line. Then nobody in it actually checked.
units.reachesYou: The stock everyone is buying at the top, the viral product, the opinion your whole group switched to in a week, five-star counts bought in bulk.
units.do: Next time you are drawn to something because it is popular, find one reason to want it that would still be true if nobody else wanted it.

scene.analogy: Picking the restaurant with the line

beats.say: Others see the line, and follow.
You join. It must be good.
B was better. Nobody tried it.
A line is not a review.

units.title: Status quo bias
units.outcome: Ask whether you would choose what you have if you were choosing today.
units.why: Whatever you already have feels safe, even when it costs more. Changing takes a small effort now; staying costs a little every month, quietly, forever.
units.reachesYou: Phone and internet plans, insurance, bank fees, the subscription you forgot, the default settings on every app, the retirement plan you never set up.
units.do: Pick one bill you have paid the same way for over a year. Spend ten minutes looking at what else is out there. Make the call if it is better.

beats.say: A plan for half the price shows up.
Every month you stay, you pay $40 more.

thaler.name: Richard Thaler
thaler.did: Described the sunk cost trap in everyday spending in 1980 and won the 2017 Nobel prize for showing how people really decide.

arkes.name: Hal Arkes
arkes.did: With Catherine Blumer in 1985, showed that theatergoers who paid full price for season tickets went to more plays than those given a discount: the money already spent pulled them back.

festinger.name: Leon Festinger
festinger.did: Named cognitive dissonance in 1957, after studying a group whose prophecy of the end of the world failed and who then believed more strongly, not less.

aronson.name: Elliot Aronson
aronson.did: Showed in 1959 that people who went through a harsh initiation to join a dull group rated the group more highly: the cost made them defend the choice.

cialdini.name: Robert Cialdini
cialdini.did: Trained as a salesman undercover to study persuasion, and named scarcity, "only a few left", as one of its main levers in Influence (1984).

przybylski.name: Andrew Przybylski
przybylski.did: Built the first scale to measure fear of missing out in 2013 and found it ties to heavier social media use and lower mood.

wason.name: Peter Wason
wason.did: In 1960 asked people to find the rule behind the numbers 2, 4, 6. Most only tested numbers that fit their first guess, and never tried one that could prove it wrong.

nickerson.name: Raymond Nickerson
nickerson.did: Gathered the evidence for confirmation bias across science, law and medicine in one review (1998) that is still the standard account.

kahneman.name: Daniel Kahneman
kahneman.did: With Amos Tversky, mapped how judgment fails in predictable ways, from anchoring to loss aversion, and won the 2002 Nobel prize in economics for it.

tversky.name: Amos Tversky
tversky.did: With Daniel Kahneman, described the availability shortcut (1973) and built prospect theory (1979), which measured that losses weigh about twice as much as equal gains.

northcraft.name: Gregory Northcraft and Margaret Neale
northcraft.did: In 1987 showed that real estate agents valued the same house higher or lower depending on the asking price they were shown, while saying the price had not swayed them.

slovic.name: Paul Slovic
slovic.did: Spent decades measuring how people judge risk, and showed that dread and vivid images, not the numbers, drive what we fear.

asch.name: Solomon Asch
asch.did: In the 1950s had people match line lengths beside actors giving a wrong answer. About a third of the time, people went along with the group against their own eyes.

shiller.name: Robert Shiller
shiller.did: Warned of the dot-com and housing bubbles before they burst by showing how prices feed on the crowd's own excitement, and won the 2013 Nobel prize in economics.

samuelson.name: William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser
samuelson.did: Named status quo bias in 1988, showing in experiments and real choices of health plans that people stick with whatever option is already theirs.

madrian.name: Brigitte Madrian
madrian.did: With Dennis Shea (2001), showed that when one company made retirement savings the default, joining went from about a third of new workers to most of them.
